content: Splicing factor 1, also referred to as zinc finger protein 162 (ZFM162), is a protein encoded by the SF1 gene in humans. This protein plays a critical role in the ATP-dependent assembly of the spliceosome complex, which is essential for RNA splicing. The SF1 gene is indispensable for the development of the bipotential gonad. However, its expression levels decrease in the genital ridge of XX mouse embryos, while it remains active in the developing testes of XY embryos. SF1, functioning as a transcription factor, is involved in the masculinization of both Leydig cells and Sertoli cells. In Sertoli cells, in conjunction with the SOX9 protein, SF1 enhances the transcription of the anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) gene. In Leydig cells, SF1 activates the gene responsible for encoding the enzyme required for testosterone synthesis. The SF1 protein has been demonstrated to interact with several other proteins, including Ewing sarcoma breakpoint region 1 (EWSR1), U2 small nuclear RNA auxiliary factor 2 (U2AF2), the testis-determining factor (TDF), and transcription elongation regulator 1 (TCERG1). These interactions highlight its multifaceted role in gene regulation and cellular processes.
